doc.title: Eddie Bert interviewed by Monk Rowe, Danbury, Connecticut, November 20, 2001

title: Benny Goodman's bebop band and the California stay
summary: Goodman's modern band with Wardell Gray and his broken six-month promise.

story.theme_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the leader and his bands
story.community_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the perfectionist bandleader

blocks.x: Jeez. And Benny was — was he making a conscious effort to maybe get a little more modern with that group?
Maybe he was I don’t know. I don’t know where he had that idea. I mean he didn’t fit in. But somehow he wanted to do that. Wardell was great.
What was it like to work with Benny, or get along with him?
Not like Stan. Well all the stories are true.

Well he took us out to California and said we were going to be there six months. Guys subletted their apartments. I had a cheap apartment so I didn’t sublet it. After six weeks he says, “I’m going to Lake Mead and I’m going fishing. And then we’re going up and down the coast for about a week or two and then we’re going back to New York.” What about the six months? So guys jumped off. Milt Bernhart was on the band. He’s from California so he just jumped off. Nick Travis drove back in a day and a half to Philadelphia, he got so mad. Straight through.
Did you have your family with you?
But it was lucky I didn’t sublet my apartment, I could send them back.
Did your kids have a sense of what you did for a living?

Well they knew what I did, I don’t know. Every time I’d go out they’d say, “have fun.” I’d say, “what do you mean, I’m going to work.” They still say that. Well I have fun but it’s still, I don’t want to let them know that.
Good thinking. You want them to think that dad is working.
